newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain protests to Portugal over freed ETA suspect.
newsitem.headline: Spain protests to Portugal over freed ETA suspect.

text.p: Spain officially protested to Portugal on Monday over a Lisbon court's refusal to hand over a suspected ETA militant.
The diplomatic row has prompted calls from Madrid for a European extradition treaty to be finalised.

The Foreign Ministry summoned Portuguese ambassador Leonardo Matheas to convey anger at the Supreme Court's rebuff last week of Spain's extradition request for Jose Luis Telletxea, wanted for supporting ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom).
"It was a formal protest to express our uneasiness with the decision of the Supreme Court," a Foreign Ministry official told Reuters.

The ambassador met Deputy Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs Jose Carvajal but no further details were immediately available. The Portuguese embassy would not comment except to confirm the meeting took place.
Telletxea is wanted in Spain for smuggling ETA rebels and weapons across the border with France. He was arrested in Lisbon in 1996 as he tried to board a flight to Venezuela with false documents.
Last Friday, Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said the Portuguese courts should have respected the opinion of Spanish courts which characterised Telletxea's actions as a crime in Spain.
Matutes said Spain was considering reestablishing border checkpoints now that Telletxea was free to prevent him crossing back into Spain with impunity and committing other crimes.
About 800 people have been killed in ETA's 29-year-old campaign for an independent Basque state. The group has stepped up attacks this year, killing six people so far including a Supreme Court judge.

Extradition is a highly sensitive issue in Spain. Officials said on Friday the row with Portugal may have been avoided had the all 15 EU members already ratified an extradition convention signed in Dublin last September.
Once the accord is finalised, countries will no longer be able to refuse extradition on grounds the offence was political.
Spain is still trying to clarify the Portuguese court's reasons for releasing Telletxea.

Portuguese Justice Minister Jose Vera Jardim told Reuters on Friday he did not yet know the full reasons for the decision but said it was final. Portuguese newspapers said the ruling was based on a lack of evidence to back Spain's case.

Meanwhile, the leader of Portugal's main opposition Social Democrat party warned at the weekend the ruling could turn the country into a refuge for violent Basque separatists and put its own security at risk.
A similar diplomatic row erupted between Madrid and Brussels last year when a Belgian court ruled against extraditing a couple suspected of collaborating in an ETA attack.
